entry: Irish singer and composer whose multi-layered vocals and music incorporating Celtic elements brought her worldwide fame. She left the family band Clannad in 1982 to pursue a solo career. Her album *Watermark* (1988) and its single "Orinoco Flow (Sail Away)" propelled her to international success. With an estimated equivalent of more than 80 million albums sold, she is the best-selling Irish solo artist and the second-best-selling music act from Ireland, after the band [[U2]]. She has won four [[Grammy Awards]].

Italian racing driver and entrepreneur who founded [[Scuderia Ferrari]] in 1929. He served in the Italian Army during [[World War I|World War I]] and began racing in 1919, joining the racing department of Alfa Romeo in 1920 and winning his first Grand Prix in 1923. In 1947 he launched the [[Ferrari]] car company in Maranello. Under his leadership in [[Formula One]], Ferrari won nine World Drivers' Championships and eight World Constructors' Championships during his lifetime. Widely known as *il Commendatore* or *il Drake*, a nickname from British opponents that referred to [[Francis Drake]], he built his small company's reputation on sporting results.

Large biological molecule, usually a [[Protein|protein]], that acts as a catalyst. Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions without being consumed, often by factors of millions. The molecules they act on are called substrates, which are converted into products. Enzymes are known to catalyze over 5,000 types of biochemical reactions, and nearly all [[Metabolism|metabolic]] processes within a cell depend on them. Their high specificity comes from their three-dimensional structure, and their activity is affected by temperature and pH. Industry uses them to produce antibiotics, and biological washing powders use them to break down protein, starch and fat stains. In 1877 the German physiologist Wilhelm Kühne first used the term enzyme.

Second epoch of the [[Paleogene]] Period in the [[Cenozoic]] Era. It began about 56 million years ago with the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, a short period of intense warming and ocean acidification, and ended at the Eocene–Oligocene transition between 33.9 and 33.4 million years ago. The epoch closed with the *Grande Coupure*, a major [[Extinction event|extinction event]]. Global climates were predominantly greenhouse-like, and the early Eocene was among the hottest intervals in Earth's history. Mammals diversified rapidly, and the first modern orders of primates and early [[Whale|whales]] appeared.

Ancient Greek city on the coast of Ionia, in present-day Selçuk, Turkey. Built in the 10th century BC by Attic and Ionian Greek colonists, it came under the control of the [[Roman Republic]] in 129 BC. Its [[Artemis|Temple of Artemis]] was one of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]]. Ephesus was one of the seven churches addressed in the [[Book of Revelation]]. Its harbour was slowly silted up by the Küçükmenderes River, and its importance as a port declined. Its ruins, a major tourist attraction, were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

Ancient Mesopotamian epic, the world's oldest surviving example of narrative literature. It derives from five Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of [[Uruk]], some of which may date to the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2100 BC). The Old Babylonian version dates to the 18th century BC. The 12-tablet Standard Babylonian version, compiled by Sîn-lēqi-unninni, dates to between the 13th and 10th centuries BC. Some of its best copies were found in the library of the Assyrian king [[Ashurbanipal]] at [[Nineveh]]. The story follows Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu, a wild man created by the gods, and Gilgamesh's quest for eternal life, which leads him to the flood survivor Utnapishtim. George Smith read translated fragments of the epic in 1872.

Lengthy narrative poem, typically about the extraordinary deeds of extraordinary characters in dealings with gods or other superhuman forces. Epic poems were originally composed and transmitted orally, learned word for word by bards. Studies of living oral traditions in the Balkans by Milman Parry and Albert Lord in the early 20th century demonstrated how such poems were constructed. Famous examples include the Sumerian [[Epic of Gilgamesh]], the Greek [[Iliad|*Iliad*]] and [[Odyssey|*Odyssey*]] attributed to Homer, Virgil's [[Aeneid|*Aeneid*]], the Old English [[Beowulf|*Beowulf*]] and Dante's [[Divine Comedy|*Divine Comedy*]]. The longest written epic from antiquity is the Indian *Mahabharata*, at about 1.8 million words.

Ancient Greek philosopher who founded the school of Epicureanism. He taught that managing one's desires, removing unnecessary fears, and cultivating friendship and virtuous living lead to a pleasant life. Like [[Democritus]], he held that all things consist of atoms moving through empty space, but he proposed an atomic "swerve" that allowed [[Free will|free will]] in an otherwise deterministic universe. He taught that the gods exist but take no part in human affairs. He founded a school, "The Garden", in [[Athens]]. Of his more than 300 works, only a few letters and the *Principal Doctrines* survive intact, so much of his philosophy is known through [[Lucretius]] and Diogenes of Oenoanda. A modified version of his ideas was revived in the 17th century by Pierre Gassendi, and his influence grew during the Enlightenment, including on [[John Locke]] and [[Karl Marx]].

Rapid spread of disease to a large number of people in a given population within a short period. An epidemic is declared when incidence rises above a baseline rate; for meningococcal infections, an attack rate above 15 cases per 100,000 people for two consecutive weeks is considered an epidemic. Epidemics are generally caused by changes in the host population, a genetic change in a pathogen, or the introduction of an emerging pathogen. A few cases of a very rare disease may count as an epidemic, while many cases of the [[Common cold|common cold]] would not. An epidemic that spreads to other countries or continents and affects a substantial number of people becomes a [[Pandemic|pandemic]]. The 2014 West Africa [[Ebola]] outbreak illustrates the high mortality that can follow when rapid intervention is absent.

Study of the distribution and determinants of disease and other health conditions in human populations. It is a cornerstone of [[Public health|public health]], identifying risk factors for disease and targets for [[Preventive healthcare|preventive healthcare]], and it shapes policy. Major areas include disease causation, transmission, outbreak investigation, surveillance and the comparison of treatment effects in clinical trials. Epidemiologists rely on biology, [[Statistics|statistics]], the social sciences and engineering. In 1854 [[John Snow]] traced a [[Cholera|cholera]] outbreak in London's Broad Street to a contaminated water pump, demonstrating waterborne transmission. Descriptive studies characterize cases by time, place and person, while analytic studies test hypotheses through cohort, case-control and randomized controlled trials. The term appears to have been first used to describe the study of epidemics in 1802 by the Spanish physician Joaquín de Villalba.

Single layer of cells that covers the [[Leaf|leaves]], flowers, roots and stems of plants. It forms the boundary between the plant and its environment, protecting against water loss, regulating gas exchange, secreting metabolic compounds and, in roots, absorbing water and mineral nutrients. The upper and lower surfaces of most leaves differ in construction and often in function. Specialized epidermal cells include the paired guard cells of [[Stoma|stomata]], which regulate openings for carbon dioxide intake and oxygen release, and trichomes, hair-like projections that deter herbivores and reduce water loss. Woody stems and some structures such as [[Potato|potato]] tubers develop a secondary covering called the periderm, which replaces the epidermis as the protective layer.

Study of changes in [[Gene expression|gene expression]] that occur without altering the [[DNA|DNA]] sequence. The prefix *epi-* implies features that lie on top of or in addition to the DNA-based mechanism of inheritance. These changes usually persist through cell division and may last for multiple generations, and they can result from environmental factors or from normal development. Mechanisms include DNA methylation and histone modification, and [[RNA|non-coding RNA]] also regulates gene expression. Epigenetic regulation drives cellular differentiation: as a fertilized egg divides, its daughter cells become [[Neuron|neurons]], muscle cells and other types by activating some genes and inhibiting others. Aberrant DNA methylation can silence tumor suppressor genes in cancers.

Study of inscriptions as writing, including the identification of graphemes, the clarification of their meanings, and the classification of their uses by date and cultural context. An epigraph can be any text, from a single mark on a pot to a lengthy document, and most inscriptions are short. Inscriptions are engraved, painted or scratched on durable materials such as stone or metal, usually for public view. Epigraphy is a primary tool of [[Archaeology|archaeology]] for literate cultures and helps identify forgeries. Epigraphists reconstruct, translate and date texts, while historians interpret the events they record. The Behistun inscription, an official document of the [[Achaemenid Empire]] engraved on rock in Iran, is one example. The modern discipline took shape in the 19th century with the *Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum*, begun in 1853 under [[Theodor Mommsen]].

Group of neurological disorders characterized by recurrent seizures, which are abnormal, excessive and synchronized electrical discharges in the brain's [[Neuron|neurons]]. Two or more unprovoked seizures define epilepsy. The cause is unknown in most cases; others follow [[Brain injury|brain injury]], [[Stroke|stroke]] or [[Brain tumor|brain tumors]], infections or birth defects, and known genetic [[Mutation|mutations]] account for a small proportion. As of 2021 about 51 million people had epilepsy, nearly 80% of them in the developing world. Seizures are controllable with medication in about 69% of cases, and surgery, neurostimulation or dietary changes may be considered for others. Many people improve enough that treatment is no longer needed. In many countries people with epilepsy face driving restrictions.

Thin, continuous, protective layer of cells that lines the outer surfaces of many organs, the inner surfaces of body cavities and blood vessels. It is one of the four basic types of animal tissue, along with [[Connective tissue|connective tissue]], [[Muscle|muscle tissue]] and [[Nervous tissue|nervous tissue]]. Its cells take three principal shapes: squamous, columnar and cuboidal. Arranged in a single layer it is called simple epithelium, and in several layers it is stratified or compound. All [[Gland|glands]] are made of epithelial cells. Epithelium has no blood vessels and receives nutrients by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue. The epidermis, the outermost layer of the [[Skin|skin]], is an example.

Instant in time chosen as the origin of a particular calendar era, serving as the reference point from which time is measured. In [[Chronology|chronology]] and periodization, an epoch is usually chosen by congruity or by convention, and is typically defined by a specific event of change. Where a historical shift is gradual, the epoch is set at the precise moment a critical threshold is crossed. More broadly, an epoch is a distinct period in history, geology or other fields, characterized by significant events or conditions.

Family of basic components or cured end products of epoxy resins, also called polyepoxides. Epoxy resins are cross-linked with co-reactants called hardeners or curatives, including polyfunctional [[Amine|amines]], [[Acid|acids]], [[Phenol|phenols]], alcohols and [[Thiol|thiols]], to form a thermosetting [[Polymer|polymer]] with strong mechanical properties and high thermal and chemical resistance. Applications include metal coatings, composites, electronics, LEDs, high-tension electrical insulators and structural [[Adhesive|adhesives]]. Exposure can cause contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and respiratory problems, especially from compounds that are not fully cured.

Virus of the [[Herpes|herpes]] family, also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), and one of the most common viruses in humans. It establishes a permanent infection in B cells and is the most common cause of [[Infectious mononucleosis|infectious mononucleosis]], accounting for 90% of cases. It was the first identified oncogenic virus and is linked to several [[Cancer|cancers]], including [[Hodgkin lymphoma|Hodgkin lymphoma]] and Burkitt lymphoma, as well as some autoimmune diseases. Most people become infected, often without symptoms in childhood. In the United States about half of five-year-old children and about 90% of adults show evidence of past infection. No [[Vaccine|vaccine]] has been approved to prevent infection.

Relation stating that two quantities or expressions have the same value, written A = B. Equality is often treated as a primitive notion, informally described as a relation each thing bears to itself and nothing else. Its reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity were understood in ancient times but were not stated symbolically until the late 19th century, by Giuseppe Peano. The equals sign was introduced by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in *The Whetstone of Witte* (1557). In logic, equality is a primitive predicate with the law of identity and the substitution property. In [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], the most common foundation of mathematics, two sets are equal if they have the same members, a principle called the axiom of extensionality.

Process of finding the values of unknown variables that make an equation true. A solution is an assignment of values to the unknowns that makes the equality hold, and the set of all solutions is the solution set. An equation may be solved numerically, admitting only numbers, or symbolically, using expressions. For example, x + y = 2x − 1 is solved for x by x = y + 1. Depending on the context, solving may mean finding any solution, all solutions, or one satisfying a further condition. Babylonians used geometric techniques for [[Quadratic equation|quadratic equations]] as early as 2000 BC. In 1824 Niels Henrik Abel proved that no general algebraic formula exists for quintic equations using radicals. Higher-degree equations are often approximated with methods such as [[Newton's method|Newton's method]].

Set of equations describing the motion of a physical system as a function of time. Its variables are usually spatial coordinates and time, and in classical mechanics the functions are defined in [[Euclidean space|Euclidean space]], while in relativity they are defined in curved spaces. If the dynamics of a system is known, its equations of motion are the solutions of the [[Differential equation|differential equations]] describing that dynamics. For constant acceleration, kinematic equations relate final velocity to initial velocity, acceleration and time: v = v₀ + at. Newton's second law expresses acceleration as net force divided by mass, and for variable forces it yields second-order differential equations that are solved numerically or analytically. Advanced formulations include Lagrange's equations and Hamilton's equations.

Circle of latitude at 0 degrees that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Halfway between the North and South Poles, it measures about 21,639 nautical miles (40,075 km; 24,902 miles) in circumference. Because noon sunlight appears almost directly overhead throughout the year, the equator has a stable daytime temperature. On the [[Equinox|equinoxes]] the sun crosses the equator at a shallow angle, and all latitudes have nearly 12 hours of day and night. The equator passes through 11 countries on land, including [[Ecuador|Ecuador]], [[Brazil|Brazil]], [[Gabon|Gabon]] and [[Kenya|Kenya]]. The equator has the fastest rotational speed of any point on Earth's surface, which makes it an advantageous site for space launches.

Country on the west coast of [[Central Africa|Central Africa]] (pop., 2025: 1,853,559), the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa. It consists of the mainland region of Río Muni, bordered by [[Cameroon|Cameroon]] and [[Gabon|Gabon]], and the islands of Bioko and Annobón. The capital has been Ciudad de la Paz since January 2026. Portugal ceded territory to Spain under the 1778 Treaty of El Pardo, and it was declared Spanish Guinea during the [[Scramble for Africa|Scramble for Africa]]. It gained independence in 1968 under the dictatorship of Francisco Macías Nguema, who was overthrown in a coup in 1979 by his nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo; Obiang has been president since. Oil production from the mid-1990s made it one of the richest countries per capita in Africa, though wealth is unevenly distributed. Foreign observers widely describe the regime as a dictatorship, and Freedom House's annual survey has consistently ranked the country among the "worst of the worst" for political and civil rights.

Celestial coordinate system widely used to specify the positions of celestial objects. It is geocentric, with its origin at the centre of Earth and its fundamental plane formed by the projection of Earth's [[Equator|equator]] onto the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]]. Its primary direction points toward the [[Equinox|March equinox]]. The system does not rotate with Earth but remains relatively fixed against the background stars. Right ascension is measured eastward from the vernal equinox, and declination north or south of the celestial equator. Because of axial precession, coordinates are specified for epochs such as J2000.0 (January 1, 2000). The system underpins the International Celestial Reference System (ICRS) in modern astronomy.

Use of horses for sport, work or recreation, including riding, driving and vaulting. Commonly called horse riding in Commonwealth English and horseback riding in American English, the term derives from Latin *equester* and *equus*, meaning horseman and horse. Chariot racing featured at the [[Olympic Games|Olympic Games]] as early as 680 BC. Modern equestrian events debuted at the 1900 Paris Olympics and became a permanent fixture from the 1912 Stockholm Games, which introduced dressage, eventing and jumping as core disciplines. The Fédération Equestre Internationale (FEI), founded in 1921, oversees the sport and represents 136 national federations. Eventing, a test of all-around riding skills, was originally developed as a military [[Cavalry|cavalry]] competition.
